why: Many companies in Tunisia and in Europe now want developers who can build features with AI: a support chatbot, extraction from documents, ticket classification. This work does not take a PhD: it takes good Python and a solid understanding of the API. This course teaches you to build applications with the Claude API the way you would in production: with a calculated cost, handled errors, and JSON you can trust.
outcome: build a Python app that talks to Claude: conversation, streaming, valid JSON, tools, caching and batches, handled errors, and logs of tokens and cost.

lessons.title: The Messages API: your first request
text: Everything in the Claude API goes through one endpoint: the Messages API (POST /v1/messages). In Python, the 'anthropic' SDK wraps it in client.messages.create. Tools, structured outputs, thinking: all of them are features of the same API, not separate APIs.

A request mainly contains: model (the model), max_tokens (the maximum length of the answer), messages (a list of messages, each with a role 'user' or 'assistant' and a content), and optionally system: the system prompt, meaning the general instructions (who you are, which language to answer in, what is forbidden).

A very important point: the API is stateless. It remembers nothing between one request and the next. If you want a conversation over several turns, you keep the history and send all of it every time. That is why the cost rises as the conversation grows: every turn you pay for the whole history again (but there is caching, covered in lesson 6).

The response is not a string: it is a Message object. response.content is a list of blocks, each with a type: 'text', 'thinking', 'tool_use'... Don't read content[0].text blindly: take the blocks whose type is 'text'. response.usage tells you how many input_tokens and output_tokens the request used, and that is what you pay for.

Then, before using the content, check response.stop_reason: 'end_turn' means it finished normally, 'max_tokens' means it was cut off (the answer is not complete), 'tool_use' means it wants to call a tool, and 'refusal' means it refused the request for safety reasons. A good app handles each case explicitly.
points: The SDK reads the API key from the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable: anthropic.Anthropic() with no argument. If you write the key in the code, it ends up on GitHub the day you commit, and anyone can use it at your expense.
The first message must have role 'user'.
The history: append the user's message, then append response.content with role 'assistant'.
Log response._request_id: when something breaks, this is what support asks for.

example.code:
import anthropic

# The SDK reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment: never write the key in code
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

SYSTEM = "You are the support assistant of a Tunisian phone shop. Answer briefly, in the customer's language."
history = []  # the API keeps no memory: we keep the conversation ourselves


def ask(user_text):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=16000,
        system=SYSTEM,
        messages=history,  # resend the whole conversation every time
    )
    if response.stop_reason == "refusal":
        history.pop()  # keep the history clean
        return "Sorry, I can't help with that."
    # content is a list of blocks: keep only the text blocks
    text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    print("stop:", response.stop_reason,
          "| in:", response.usage.input_tokens,
          "| out:", response.usage.output_tokens)
    return text


print(ask("Aslema, 9adeh soum forfait 20 Go?"))
print(ask("W ken nzid 10 Go o5rin, 9adeh walla?"))  # works because history was resent
example.note: The second turn understands '10 more GB' because the history of the first turn was sent with it.

lessons.title: Which model and how much effort? The cost of each request
text: Choosing the model is the first decision that involves money. In October 2026 the current models are: Claude Opus 5.5 ('claude-opus-5-5') is the default, 1M tokens of context and 128K of output, at $4 input and $20 output per million tokens. Claude Sonnet 5.5 ('claude-sonnet-5-5') at $2 / $10, good for large volumes. Claude Haiku 5.5 ('claude-haiku-5-5') at $0.10 / $0.50 (for prompts of 100K tokens or less), for small, fast work: classification, routing, extraction. And there is Claude Fable 5.1 ('claude-fable-5-1'), the most capable, at $10 / $50. Write these ids exactly as they are, with no date.

The calculation is simple: cost = (input_tokens x input price + output_tokens x output price) / 1,000,000. Example: a request with 2,000 input tokens and 500 output on Opus 5.5 = (2000 x 4 + 500 x 20) / 1,000,000 = $0.018. Multiply it by 10,000 messages a day and you see why you must calculate before you deploy.

New models think before they answer (adaptive thinking). On Opus 5.5 thinking is always on and you cannot turn it off: the control is output_config={'effort': ...} with 'low', 'medium', 'high', 'xhigh' or 'max'. The default on Opus 5.5 is 'medium'. Less effort = fewer tokens = cheaper and faster, but it can lower quality on hard work. Thinking counts against max_tokens and is added to the output you pay for.

Some old parameters no longer work on new models: temperature, top_p, top_k, budget_tokens, and prefill (starting the answer with an assistant message). If you send them, the API returns 400. If you find an old tutorial with temperature=0.2, this is why it doesn't work.

The right method: start with Opus 5.5 at the default effort, build a set of examples whose correct answer you know, then try lower effort or Sonnet/Haiku. If the quality holds, keep the cheaper one. Don't change models blindly.
points: client.messages.count_tokens(model=..., messages=...) counts the input tokens for you before you send.
Haiku 5.5 is good for classification and routing; Opus 5.5 for reasoning and agents.
Prices change: keep the price table in a single config and check it before production.

example.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# USD per 1M tokens (input, output) - check the pricing page before you rely on it
PRICES = {
    "claude-opus-5-5": (4.00, 20.00),
    "claude-sonnet-5-5": (2.00, 10.00),
    "claude-haiku-5-5": (0.10, 0.50),  # for prompts up to 100K tokens
}


def cost_usd(model, usage):
    price_in, price_out = PRICES[model]
    return (usage.input_tokens * price_in + usage.output_tokens * price_out) / 1_000_000


def classify(message, model="claude-haiku-5-5"):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=model,
        max_tokens=1024,  # thinking also counts toward max_tokens
        output_config={"effort": "low"},  # low | medium | high | xhigh | max
        system="Classify the customer message. Answer with one word: billing, network, sales or other.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": message}],
    )
    label = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text").strip()
    return label, cost_usd(model, response.usage)


label, cost = classify("El connexion ta7et men sbe7, w zeda el facture tal3a!")
print(label, f"${cost:.6f}")

# Before sending a big document, count its tokens (this call is free of output)
with open("contract.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    count = client.messages.count_tokens(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f.read()}],
    )
print("input tokens:", count.input_tokens)
example.note: contract.txt is an example file; don't send personal data unless it is needed.

lessons.title: Streaming: the answer comes out word by word
text: If an answer takes 20 seconds, the user sees an empty screen and thinks the app is broken. Streaming sends the text as it is written, like in a chat. The total time doesn't change, but the user sees something in under a second, and that changes the whole experience.

In Python, the recommended helper is client.messages.stream(...) with with. Inside it, stream.text_stream gives you the pieces of text one by one. When it ends, stream.get_final_message() returns the complete Message, just like messages.create: content, stop_reason, usage. So you don't have to collect the tokens yourself.

Why not always messages.create? Because long answers can take more than 10 minutes. The SDK rejects a non-streaming request when it estimates it will take a long time (ValueError), and connections that stay idle for a long time get dropped. So when max_tokens is large (for example 64000), use streaming. If you don't need the text word by word, you can use stream and get_final_message() only: you get the protection of streaming without dealing with events.

If you want finer detail, you write 'for event in stream' and look at the types: message_start, content_block_start, content_block_delta (with text_delta), content_block_stop, message_delta (with stop_reason and usage), message_stop.

In a web app (FastAPI, Django...), the idea is the same: the server reads Claude's stream and sends each piece to the browser (Server-Sent Events or WebSocket). If the user's internet connection is weak, as sometimes happens, streaming lets them see something before it drops. And if the stream breaks in the middle, you have an incomplete answer: don't save it as a complete one.
points: print(text, end='', flush=True): flush makes the text appear immediately.
For async: AsyncAnthropic() and 'async with client.messages.stream(...)' and 'async for text in stream.text_stream'.
After the stream, check final.stop_reason as always before saving the answer to the history.
Errors in the stream: catch anthropic.APIConnectionError and anthropic.APIStatusError as with ordinary requests.

example.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


def stream_answer(history):
    with client.messages.stream(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=64000,
        system="You are a patient Python tutor. Answer in Tunisian Derja written in Latin letters.",
        messages=history,
    ) as stream:
        for text in stream.text_stream:
            print(text, end="", flush=True)  # show each piece as soon as it arrives
        final = stream.get_final_message()  # the full Message, like messages.create returns
    print()
    print("stop:", final.stop_reason, "| out tokens:", final.usage.output_tokens)
    return final


history = [{"role": "user", "content": "Fasserli el list comprehension b mithel sghir."}]
final = stream_answer(history)
if final.stop_reason != "refusal":
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": final.content})

lessons.title: Structured outputs: JSON you can trust
text: Many apps don't need text, they need data: a category, an urgency, an amount, a date. We used to write 'answer me in JSON' in the prompt and hope: sometimes it added a sentence before the JSON, sometimes it forgot a field. Structured outputs solve this problem: you give a JSON schema, and the answer always comes out as valid JSON for that schema.

There are two ways. The easiest in Python: client.messages.parse(..., output_format=Ticket) with a Pydantic model. The SDK turns the class into a schema, and response.parsed_output returns a validated Ticket instance. The second way: messages.create with output_config={'format': {'type': 'json_schema', 'schema': {...}}} and then json.loads on the text. 'format' and 'effort' live together in the same output_config.

The schema has limits: every object must have additionalProperties false; enum, anyOf and $ref work; but minimum, maximum, minLength and recursive schemas do not. The Python SDK removes these constraints from the schema it sends and enforces them on the client side. The first time you use a new schema there is a compilation delay, then it is cached for 24 hours.

But careful: valid JSON does not mean correct JSON. The schema guarantees the format, not the meaning. The model can choose a wrong category or set urgency 'high' on an ordinary message. So add business checks (your own rules), and for unusual cases, let a person review.

Also: if stop_reason is 'refusal', the output may not follow the schema; if 'max_tokens', the JSON may be cut off. Always check the stop_reason before using the data. Strict tool use (tools with strict: true) is covered in lesson 5.
points: Literal['low', 'medium', 'high'] in Pydantic becomes an enum in the schema.
Structured outputs work with Batches, streaming and token counting; they don't work with citations or prefill.
Save the examples where the data was wrong: they become tests (an eval set) for your prompt.

example.code:
from typing import Literal

import anthropic
from pydantic import BaseModel

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


class Ticket(BaseModel):
    category: Literal["billing", "network", "sales", "other"]
    urgency: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]
    language: Literal["derja", "french", "arabic", "mixed"]
    summary_fr: str
    customer_is_angry: bool


response = client.messages.parse(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    system="Turn the customer message into a support ticket. summary_fr: one short sentence in French.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "3 ayem w ana bla internet, el modem yechta3el ama mafamma 7atta connexion!!"}],
    output_format=Ticket,
)

if response.stop_reason == "refusal":
    raise RuntimeError("refused: do not trust the output")
if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
    raise RuntimeError("cut off: raise max_tokens")

ticket = response.parsed_output  # a validated Ticket instance
print(ticket.category, ticket.urgency, ticket.summary_fr)

# Business checks that a schema cannot express
if ticket.urgency == "high" and ticket.category == "other":
    print("send to a human for review")

lessons.title: Tool use: let Claude use your functions
text: Claude doesn't know where a customer's order is: that information is in your database. Tool use lets you tell the model: 'there is a function called get_order_status, which takes an order_id'. When it needs it, Claude doesn't run it itself: it returns a tool_use block with the tool's name and the arguments, and stop_reason = 'tool_use'. Your code is what runs the function and returns the result.

A tool is defined by a name, a description and an input_schema (a JSON schema). The description matters a lot: Claude chooses the tool based on it, so write it clearly: what it does, when to use it, an example of the arguments. Add 'strict': True so the arguments are always valid for the schema (and additionalProperties false is required).

The loop: (1) send the messages with tools; (2) if stop_reason is 'tool_use', add response.content to the history with role assistant; (3) for each tool_use block, run the tool and build a tool_result with the same tool_use_id; (4) send all the results in a single user message; (5) repeat until stop_reason is no longer 'tool_use'. Claude can request several tools in the same turn (parallel): all the results go in the same message.

When the tool fails (the order doesn't exist, an API is down), don't let the app crash: return a tool_result with 'is_error': True and a clear message. Claude reads it and explains to the user or tries another way.

The SDK also has a tool runner (beta): you write a Python function with @beta_tool, and client.beta.messages.tool_runner(...) runs the loop by itself. It saves time; the manual loop gives you more control. Careful: on Opus 5.5, a forced tool_choice ('any' or 'tool') returns 400; leave it at 'auto' and say in the prompt which tool it should use. And a tool's arguments are model output: validate them before touching data or files.
points: Every tool_result must have the tool_use_id of the block it answers.
Put a limit on the loop (for example 10 turns) so it doesn't run forever.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a protocol for connecting ready-made tool servers to Claude; Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK are other products with built-in tools.

example.code:
import json

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

ORDERS = {"TN-1042": {"status": "shipped", "city": "Sfax"}}

tools = [{
    "name": "get_order_status",
    "description": "Get the delivery status of a customer order by its id, for example TN-1042.",
    "strict": True,  # Claude's arguments always match the schema
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["order_id"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}]


def run_tool(name, args):
    """Return (content, is_error). Our code runs the tool, not Claude."""
    if name == "get_order_status":
        order = ORDERS.get(args["order_id"])
        if order is None:
            return f"No order with id {args['order_id']}", True
        return json.dumps(order), False
    return f"Unknown tool {name}", True


messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Win wsolt el commande mte3i TN-1042?"}]

for _ in range(10):  # safety cap: never loop forever
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=16000,
        tools=tools,
        messages=messages,
    )
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break  # end_turn, max_tokens or refusal: nothing to run
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    results = []
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            content, failed = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
            results.append({
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id,  # must match the tool_use block
                "content": content,
                "is_error": failed,
            })
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})  # all results in ONE user message

print(response.stop_reason)
print("".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

lessons.title: Prompt caching and Batches: lower the cost and the latency
text: If every request sends the same 20,000-token FAQ, you pay for it every time. Prompt caching lets the API reuse a prefix it has already read. Reading from the cache costs about 0.1x the input price (on Opus 5.5: $0.20 per million, so 0.05x), and it is faster.

Caching matches on the prefix: the order is tools, then system, then messages. Any byte that changes in the prefix invalidates the cache for everything after it. So put the fixed things first and the changing things last. You set a breakpoint with 'cache_control': {'type': 'ephemeral'} on the last fixed block (max 4 breakpoints). The cache lives 5 minutes by default (each read renews them), or one hour with 'ttl': '1h'. There is also a top-level cache_control on the request that places the breakpoint by itself, good for conversations.

Writing to the cache costs more: 1.25x for 5 minutes, 2x for one hour. So it only pays off when the prefix is repeated. And there is a minimum: on the new models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) the prefix must be at least 512 tokens, otherwise it isn't cached and you get no error either.

How do you know it works? Look at response.usage: cache_creation_input_tokens (written to the cache), cache_read_input_tokens (read from the cache), input_tokens (the rest at full price). If cache_read is always 0, something is changing the prefix: datetime.now() in the system prompt, a user id, json.dumps without sort_keys, tools that change.

The Batches API is something else: you send many requests at once (up to 100,000 or 256 MB), they are processed asynchronously, and you pay 50% less. Most batches finish within an hour, 24 hours at most, and the results stay available for 29 days. Good for work that can wait: classifying a whole day's tickets, translating a catalogue, evaluating a prompt. Not for chat: the user won't wait an hour.
points: Total prompt = input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens.
Parallel requests with the same prefix can't read a cache that is still being written: send one, then the rest.
Batch: client.messages.batches.create, then retrieve until processing_status == 'ended', then results.

example.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# A long FAQ that stays byte-identical between requests (no date, no user id inside)
with open("faq_shop.md", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    FAQ = f.read()

SYSTEM = [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Answer customer questions using only the FAQ below."},
    {"type": "text", "text": FAQ, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},  # breakpoint after the stable part
]


def answer(question):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=16000,
        system=SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],  # the varying part comes last
    )
    u = response.usage
    print(f"cache write={u.cache_creation_input_tokens} "
          f"cache read={u.cache_read_input_tokens} uncached={u.input_tokens}")
    return "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")


answer("Kifech nbaddel l'adresse de livraison?")   # 1st call: writes the cache
answer("9addeh ta5ou el livraison l Gabes?")       # within 5 minutes: reads the cache
example.note: The first call writes the cache; the second, if it comes within 5 minutes and the FAQ is over 512 tokens, reads from it.

lessons.title: Errors, retries, rate limits and refusals
text: In production, the API sometimes returns an error: 429 when you exceed the rate limit (requests or tokens per minute), 500 or 529 when the service is struggling or overloaded, a timeout when the network is slow. A good app doesn't crash: it separates what deserves a retry from what doesn't.

The Python SDK retries by itself (with exponential backoff) on connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and >= 500, twice by default. You change this with max_retries on the client or with client.with_options(max_retries=5) for one request. The default timeout is 10 minutes; you can set timeout=60.0, and when it is exceeded anthropic.APITimeoutError is raised.

Exceptions have classes: BadRequestError (400, the request is wrong: don't retry, fix the code), AuthenticationError (401, the key is wrong or missing), PermissionDeniedError (403), NotFoundError (404, often a wrong model id), RateLimitError (429), InternalServerError (>= 500), APIConnectionError (network). All of them (except APIConnectionError) inherit from APIStatusError. Catch from the most specific to the most general: the specific ones first, and APIStatusError last.

When RateLimitError persists after the retries, the 'retry-after' header tells you how long to wait. Don't write a loop that retries without limit: set a limit, and if traffic is high, use a queue or reduce concurrency.

A refusal is not an error: the request goes through (200), but stop_reason = 'refusal' and response.stop_details may tell you the category. Each model has safety classifiers. The app must check the stop_reason before reading the content and give the user a clear message, not cut-off JSON or an empty screen. And always log the _request_id: when you talk to support it becomes your evidence.
points: Retry: 429, 500, 529, timeout, network. Don't retry: 400, 401, 403, 404.
max_retries=0 turns off the SDK's retries (if you have your own retry system).
Don't do string matching on error messages: use the classes.

example.code:
import logging

import anthropic

log = logging.getLogger("support-bot")

# The SDK already retries connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and >=500 with backoff
client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=4, timeout=60.0)


def safe_reply(messages):
    try:
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5",
            max_tokens=16000,
            messages=messages,
        )
    except anthropic.BadRequestError as e:      # 400: our request is wrong, retrying will not help
        log.error("bad request: %s", e.message)
        raise
    except anthropic.AuthenticationError:       # 401: missing or wrong ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
        log.critical("check ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
        raise
    except anthropic.RateLimitError as e:       # 429 still failing after the SDK retries
        log.warning("rate limited, retry-after=%s", e.response.headers.get("retry-after"))
        return None
    except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:       # any other non-2xx: 5xx, 529 overloaded...
        log.error("API error %s", e.status_code)
        return None
    except anthropic.APITimeoutError:           # no answer within the timeout
        log.warning("timeout")
        return None
    except anthropic.APIConnectionError:        # network problem before any response
        log.warning("network error")
        return None

    log.info("request_id=%s stop=%s", response._request_id, response.stop_reason)
    if response.stop_reason == "refusal":
        return "Sorry, I can't help with this request."
    if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
        log.warning("answer cut off at max_tokens")
    return "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")

lessons.title: Complete project: an API that creates tickets from messages in Derja/French/Arabic
text: Now we put everything together in one app. The case: a Tunisian online shop receives customer messages on Messenger or WhatsApp, in Derja (in Arabic or Latin letters), in French, in Arabic, or mixed. The job: turn each message into a structured ticket (category, urgency, language, order number, summary in French and in Arabic) so the support team can work with it.

The architecture: a FastAPI endpoint POST /tickets. It receives the message, sends it to Claude with a fixed system prompt, a structured output with a schema, and effort 'low' because the extraction is easy. We chose Sonnet 5.5: cheaper than Opus, and very good at volume. If the volume is very large and the tickets are simple, try Haiku 5.5 on an eval set before you switch.

The JSON comes out valid for the schema, but we add Ticket.model_validate_json so the data is checked on our side too. When the stop_reason is not 'end_turn' (refusal or max_tokens), we return 422 and don't output cut-off data. API errors become clear 502/503 responses for the front end.

We log every request: request_id, stop_reason, input/output tokens, cache reads, and the cost in dollars. With these logs you know how much a ticket costs, and you see whether caching works. The system prompt has cache_control, but it is only cached once it reaches 512 tokens or more (for example when you add examples).

To go further: write an eval set of 50 real messages (after removing personal data) with the correct ticket for each one, and rerun it after every change to the prompt or the model. Remove phone numbers and national ID numbers before sending unless they are needed. And let a person review tickets with urgency 'high'. That is the difference between a demo and a product.
points: Run: pip install anthropic fastapi uvicorn, then uvicorn app:app.
Test: curl or Postman with JSON {'message': '...'} on /tickets.
Optional[str] in Pydantic and anyOf [string, null] in the schema: the same idea.
For large volumes that aren't urgent: send the same request through the Batches API for 50% less.

example.code:
# app.py - run with: uvicorn app:app
# pip install anthropic fastapi uvicorn ; set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment
import logging
from typing import Literal, Optional

import anthropic
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
log = logging.getLogger("tickets")

MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
PRICE_IN, PRICE_OUT, PRICE_CACHE_READ = 2.00, 10.00, 0.20  # USD per 1M tokens

client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=3, timeout=60.0)
app = FastAPI()

SYSTEM = [{
    "type": "text",
    "text": (
        "You turn customer messages of a Tunisian online shop into support tickets. "
        "Messages can be in Tunisian Derja (Arabic or Latin letters), French, Arabic or a mix. "
        "summary_fr: one sentence in French. summary_ar: one sentence in Modern Standard Arabic. "
        "Never invent an order id: use null when the message has none."
    ),
    # only cached once the prefix reaches the model minimum (512 tokens), e.g. after adding examples
    "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
}]

TICKET_SCHEMA = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["delivery", "payment", "product", "account", "other"]},
        "urgency": {"type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high"]},
        "language": {"type": "string", "enum": ["derja", "french", "arabic", "mixed"]},
        "order_id": {"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]},
        "summary_fr": {"type": "string"},
        "summary_ar": {"type": "string"},
    },
    "required": ["category", "urgency", "language", "order_id", "summary_fr", "summary_ar"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}


class Ticket(BaseModel):
    category: Literal["delivery", "payment", "product", "account", "other"]
    urgency: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]
    language: Literal["derja", "french", "arabic", "mixed"]
    order_id: Optional[str]
    summary_fr: str
    summary_ar: str


class Incoming(BaseModel):
    message: str


@app.post("/tickets", response_model=Ticket)
def create_ticket(body: Incoming):
    try:
        response = client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL,
            max_tokens=4000,
            system=SYSTEM,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body.message}],
            output_config={
                "effort": "low",  # simple extraction: low effort is enough
                "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": TICKET_SCHEMA},
            },
        )
    except anthropic.RateLimitError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Busy, try again in a minute")
    except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:
        log.error("anthropic error %s", e.status_code)
        raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail="AI service error")
    except anthropic.APIConnectionError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail="AI service unreachable")

    u = response.usage
    cache_read = u.cache_read_input_tokens or 0
    cache_write = u.cache_creation_input_tokens or 0
    cost = (u.input_tokens * PRICE_IN + u.output_tokens * PRICE_OUT
            + cache_read * PRICE_CACHE_READ + cache_write * PRICE_IN * 1.25) / 1_000_000
    log.info("request_id=%s stop=%s in=%s out=%s cache_read=%s cost=$%.5f",
             response._request_id, response.stop_reason,
             u.input_tokens, u.output_tokens, cache_read, cost)

    if response.stop_reason != "end_turn":  # refusal or max_tokens: no reliable JSON
        raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail="Could not build a ticket")
    text = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    try:
        return Ticket.model_validate_json(text)  # validate again on our side
    except ValidationError:
        log.exception("invalid ticket JSON")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail="Could not build a ticket")

exercises.q: Write a function text_of(response) that returns the text of a Message, but raises if the model refused or the answer was cut off.
exercises.hint: Check stop_reason first, then join the blocks whose type is 'text'.

exercises.q: Which model would you choose and why: (a) classifying 50,000 short messages every night, (b) an agent working on a large code repo, (c) a customer support chatbot with medium volume?
exercises.hint: Think about cost, speed, and whether the work can wait.
exercises.answer: (a) Haiku 5.5 with effort 'low' in the Batches API: easy work, large volume, not urgent, and the batch halves the price. (b) Opus 5.5 (or Fable 5.1 if the work is very hard): long reasoning and many tools, and one mistake costs more than the tokens. (c) Sonnet 5.5 with streaming and caching on the system prompt: good quality at half the price of Opus. And in every case, compare on an eval set before deciding.

exercises.q: Write request_cost(model, usage) that calculates the cost in dollars including the cache (a 5-minute write = 1.25x the input price) for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5.
exercises.hint: The cache fields can be None: use 'or 0'.
exercises.answer:
PRICES = {  # USD per 1M tokens: input, output, cache read
    "claude-opus-5-5": (4.00, 20.00, 0.20),
    "claude-sonnet-5-5": (2.00, 10.00, 0.20),
}


def request_cost(model, usage):
    p_in, p_out, p_read = PRICES[model]
    write = (usage.cache_creation_input_tokens or 0) * p_in * 1.25  # 5-minute cache write
    read = (usage.cache_read_input_tokens or 0) * p_read
    return (usage.input_tokens * p_in + usage.output_tokens * p_out + write + read) / 1_000_000

exercises.q: Rewrite the get_order_status example with the SDK's tool runner instead of the manual loop.
exercises.hint: @beta_tool builds the schema from the signature and the docstring.
exercises.answer:
import anthropic
from anthropic import beta_tool

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
ORDERS = {"TN-1042": "shipped", "TN-2077": "preparing"}


@beta_tool
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Get the delivery status of a customer order.

    Args:
        order_id: Order id such as TN-1042.
    """
    status = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if status is None:
        return f"Error: no order with id {order_id}"
    return status


runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    tools=[get_order_status],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Chnoua a7wel el commande TN-2077?"}],
)
last = None
for message in runner:  # the SDK runs the tool loop for us
    last = message
print("".join(b.text for b in last.content if b.type == "text"))

exercises.q: Your cache_read_input_tokens is always 0, even though the FAQ is large and you send it every time. Give 4 possible causes.
exercises.answer: 1) Something changes in the prefix: datetime.now(), a uuid or a user id in the system prompt. 2) json.dumps without sort_keys, or tools that change or whose order changes. 3) The prefix is under 512 tokens, or the breakpoint was placed after the part that changes (the question) instead of before it. 4) More than 5 minutes passed between requests (the TTL), or you changed the model or the effort, or parallel requests were all writing to the cache at the same time.

exercises.q: Write a script that sends 3 customer messages in a Batch with Haiku 5.5 to classify them, waits, and prints the result.
exercises.hint: Request + MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming, then retrieve and results.
exercises.answer:
import time

import anthropic
from anthropic.types.message_create_params import MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming
from anthropic.types.messages.batch_create_params import Request

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
texts = ["El commande ma wsletch", "Nheb nbaddel el mot de passe", "Prix mte3 el casque?"]

batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=[
    Request(
        custom_id=f"msg-{i}",
        params=MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming(
            model="claude-haiku-5-5",
            max_tokens=1024,
            output_config={"effort": "low"},
            system="Answer with one word: delivery, account, sales or other.",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}],
        ),
    )
    for i, text in enumerate(texts)
])

while client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id).processing_status != "ended":
    time.sleep(60)  # most batches end within 1 hour, at most 24 hours

for result in client.messages.batches.results(batch.id):
    if result.result.type == "succeeded":
        msg = result.result.message
        print(result.custom_id, next((b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text"), ""))
    else:
        print(result.custom_id, "not done:", result.result.type)  # errored, canceled, expired

exercises.q: A customer sends: 'ena Mohamed, CIN 0xxxxxxx, num 2x xxx xxx, el commande ma wsletch'. What do you do before sending the message to the API, and why?
exercises.answer: Remove or mask the personal data the model doesn't need (national ID, phone) with a regex or a mask before the request, and keep only what the ticket needs. Why: less data leaving your system = less risk (leaks, logs, legal obligations such as data protection in Tunisia and the GDPR if you have customers in Europe). And don't log the full message; log the request_id and the tokens.

pitfalls: Writing the API key in the code or in a committed file: use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment, and if it leaks, revoke it immediately.

Reading response.content[0].text directly: the first block can be thinking, and if stop_reason is 'refusal' or 'max_tokens' the text is not complete. Check the stop_reason and filter on type == 'text'.
Using an old tutorial: temperature, top_p, budget_tokens, prefill or a forced tool_choice on Opus 5.5 return 400. Effort and the prompt are the controls now.
Putting a date, a time or a user id in the system prompt: the prefix changes with every request and caching never works.
Forgetting that the API is stateless: not sending the history, or sending tool_results in separate messages or with the wrong tool_use_id.
Trusting the JSON because it is 'valid': the schema guarantees the format, not the meaning. Add business checks and an eval set.
A very small max_tokens: thinking counts against it, and the answer comes out cut off with stop_reason 'max_tokens'.

interview.q: What does it mean that the Messages API is stateless, and how do you handle a long conversation?
interview.a: The server remembers nothing between requests: every time we send the whole history. Cost and latency grow with the length of the conversation, so we use prompt caching (a fixed prefix, a breakpoint on the last turn), and when it gets very long, a summary or compaction (beta) on the server side. And we keep the history append-only so the cache and thinking work.

interview.q: How do you lower the cost of an LLM application?
interview.a: First I measure: I log the usage of every request. Then: prompt caching for the fixed parts, the Batches API (50%) for work that isn't urgent, lower effort if the eval says the quality holds, and then a cheaper model (Sonnet or Haiku). I measure every change on an eval set, not by feel.

We define the tools with a JSON schema. The model returns tool_use blocks and stop_reason 'tool_use'. My code runs the functions, returns tool_results with the same tool_use_id, all in a single user message, and repeats until the model finishes. When a tool fails we return is_error true. We use strict true, a limit on the number of turns, and we validate the arguments before any action that has an effect.

interview.q: How do you get JSON you can trust?
interview.a: Structured outputs: output_config.format with a JSON schema or messages.parse with Pydantic. Then I check the stop_reason (refusal or max_tokens means I don't trust it), and I add business validation, because the schema guarantees the format, not correctness.

interview.q: Which errors do you retry and which not?
interview.a: I retry 429, 500, 529, timeouts and network errors with exponential backoff and a limit (the SDK does it twice by default). I don't retry 400, 401, 403, 404: the problem is in the request or the key, and a retry changes nothing. And a refusal is not an error: the request is valid, and we must answer the user with a clear message.

interview.q: What is prompt caching and how do you know it works?
interview.a: The API reuses a prefix it has already read (tools, system, messages in that order) at a much lower read price. We put cache_control on the last fixed block. We check with usage.cache_read_input_tokens: if it is always 0, something is changing in the prefix or the prefix is too small. And we add an automated test that an identical second request must read from the cache.

In chat interfaces, so the user sees the answer immediately, and when the output is long (a large max_tokens) to avoid timeouts. With get_final_message() we get the complete Message with usage and stop_reason.

interview.q: How do you know a change to the prompt didn't break anything?
interview.a: With an eval set: real (anonymised) examples with the expected result, which we run after every change (prompt, model, effort) and compare score and cost. For extraction, we compare field by field; for free text, a rubric or human review on a sample. Without an eval, every change is judged by feel.
